notable_claims: The University of Nebraska at Lincoln removed alt.* newsgroups citing pornography, though students claimed the server was running under capacity.
Princeton's computing guidelines were noted to ban speech that would be protected by the Constitution at a public university.
Questions were raised regarding the legal line between intellectual discourse and intent to hack when possessing source code for cracking programs.
classification.summary: This is an abstract for the CAF-News digest covering various issues of academic computer freedom. It highlights disputes over the removal of alt.* newsgroups at the University of Nebraska at Lincoln and critiques of computing resource guidelines at Princeton and Virginia Tech. The digest also touches upon privacy concerns regarding telnet/email logging and the legality of possessing cracking programs.
classification.title: Article 0 -- Abstract of CAF-News 02.20

notable_claims: UNL removed 'alt' newsgroups to avoid potential conflict with the federal government regarding NSFNET acceptable use policies.
The university administration claimed that some alt groups contained material on torture and mutilation.
Student representatives argued there was no evidence that the removal of these groups was forced upon the university by external authorities.
organizations: Nebraska University Students for Electronic Freedom
classification.summary: The University of Nebraska-Lincoln's Computing Resource Center stopped supplying the 'alt' hierarchy of Usenet news groups to campus computers. Director Doug Gale cited concerns over pornography and violent content, claiming that maintaining these groups risked violating NSFNET's acceptable use policy and losing federal internet access. Student representatives challenged this as censorship, arguing the university is obligated to promote freedom of expression.
classification.title: Official says messages contained pornography

notable_claims: The news server was running at 41% capacity, contradicting claims of resource exhaustion.
The CRC's 'resource issue' was actually a lack of manpower to monitor and approve unmoderated alt.* groups.
UNL claimed no censorship occurred because material remained available via anonymous FTP.
classification.summary: David Burchell challenges the University of Nebraska-Lincoln's (UNL) claim that resource constraints justified the removal of alt.* newsgroups. He argues that the actual constraint was a lack of manpower to monitor and censor content rather than technical capacity. The author suggests that expiring news more quickly would be a viable alternative to total censorship.
classification.title: Alternate ways of managing resources at UNL

identity.subject: Article 2--Alternate ways of managing resources at UNL

notable_claims: The definition of 'fighting words' has narrowed since Chaplinsky v. New Hampshire (1942).
Speech must generally be delivered face-to-face and evoke an immediate breach of peace to be excluded from First Amendment protection.
Government cannot shut off discourse solely to protect others from hearing objectionable speech unless substantial privacy interests are invaded.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie contributes to a discussion on the legal definitions of 'fighting words' and hate speech. He argues that current First Amendment interpretations require speech to be delivered one-to-one and likely to provoke immediate violence to lose protection. The post cites several Supreme Court cases to distinguish between offensive speech and speech that justifies government intervention.
classification.title: Article 3--Re: "Hate Speech" distinguished from "Panic-Inducing Speech"

notable_claims: Vague speech restrictions regarding 'unwarranted annoyance' may be unconstitutional.
Restrictions on using university systems for partisan political purposes should only exist if based on law or regulation.
The right to search files on university systems must be constrained by the Fourth Amendment's prohibition against unreasonable searches and seizures.
Due process is better served when disciplinary actions follow established student/employee handbooks rather than arbitrary computer center suspensions.
classification.summary: Carl Kadie provides a legal and civil liberties critique of Virginia Tech's proposed 'Appropriate Use of Information Systems' policy. He argues that vague restrictions on speech, political activity, and 'personal gain' may violate First Amendment rights. He also emphasizes the need for clear authorization procedures for system searches to prevent unreasonable search and seizure.
classification.title: Re: Sacrificial Lamb: An Acceptable Usage Statement for your review

identity.subject: Article 4--Re: Sacrificial Lamb: An Acceptable Usage Statement for your review

notable_claims: Electronic messages must meet the same distribution standards as tangible documents
Altering attribution of origin in electronic mail is considered a transgression of university rules
classification.summary: The item provides excerpts from Princeton University's computing resource guidelines, which link network behavior to the university's general code of conduct. It specifically mandates that electronic communications meet the same standards as tangible documents and prohibits the alteration of 'From' lines or attribution of origin.
classification.title: Excerpts from Princeton's Guidelines for the use of Campus and Network Computing Resources

notable_claims: Princeton's guidelines ban certain speech protected at state universities
Princeton explicitly treats computer speech as traditional speech
classification.summary: Carl Kadie comments on the computing resource guidelines at Princeton University. He argues that while the university bans speech that would be protected by the Constitution at state institutions, it is significant that they treat computer-based speech as traditional speech.
classification.title: Re: Excerpts from Princeton's "Guidelines ... Computing Resources"

notable_claims: The Vice President of Student Affairs claimed that allowing the photo could potentially hurt freedom of the press on campus.
The Student Press Law Center and a local newspaper editor did not consider the photo obscene.
classification.summary: A report regarding a controversy at the University of Southwestern Louisiana over a nude photograph published in the student yearbook. The item outlines conflicting views on whether the content was obscene and discusses the role of campus administration in censorship.
classification.title: Nude photo in yearbook stirs campus debate

identity.subject: Article 7--"Nude photo in yearbook stirs campus debate"

notable_claims: A parody of a deceased feminist professor's work caused a significant split among Harvard Law faculty.
The parody suggested the original author was published due to her marriage to a Harvard professor rather than merit.
classification.summary: A Usenet discussion regarding a controversy at Harvard Law School where students published a parody of an article by the late Professor Mary Joe Frug. The author argues that the parody was offensive not only because it targeted a deceased person and feminism, but because it questioned Frug's professional merit based on her marriage. The post contrasts this faculty reaction with other 'un-Ivy' behaviors, such as a physical assault on speaker Adolfo Calero.
classification.title: Article 8--Re: UPI story: Parody splits Harvard Law faculty

identity.subject: Article 8--Re: UPI story: Parody splits Harvard Law faculty

notable_claims: Logging outgoing telnet sessions is compared to phone company record keeping for the purpose of identifying hacking.
In Finland (as of 1992), police access to phone records was not legal but being proposed.
classification.summary: A discussion regarding the ethics and legality of logging outgoing telnet sessions, comparing network logs to telephone company records. Hank Nussbacher argues that such logs are necessary for detecting hacking and generally ignored unless a crime is suspected. Jyrki Kuoppala adds a perspective on Finnish privacy laws and police access to financial and telecommunications data.
classification.title: Article 9--Surveillance of phone calling records

notable_claims: Possession of cracker programs may lead to scrutiny similar to carrying lock-picks.
Outlawing cracking software raises concerns about the boundary between intellectual discourse and criminal intent.
classification.summary: A discussion on the legality and ethics of possessing 'cracker programs' compared to physical lock-picking tools. The author questions whether outlawing such software would inadvertently criminalize intellectual discourse, security research papers, or the discussion of cracking methods.
